entries.sentence: Prostate symptoms are mostly urinary, such as a weak flow or going more often.
entries.note: Urinary symptoms main sign; examples from NHS summaries.

entries.sentence: Causes include enlargement, infection and cancer, and a GP can assess them.
entries.note: Enlargement, infection (prostatitis) and cancer causes covered in NHS pages.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes urinary changes, such as a weak flow, trouble starting and needing to go more often, as the main signs of an enlarged prostate.
entries.note: As in body section ledger entries.

entries.sentence: An enlarged prostate is not cancer and does not raise the risk of prostate cancer, but a man can have both at once.
entries.note: As in body section ledger entries.

entries.sentence: Early prostate cancer often causes no symptoms, according to the NHS.
entries.note: As in body section ledger entries.

entries.sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP about difficulty peeing, blood in the pee, pain when peeing or not being able to pee.
entries.note: As in body section ledger entries.

entries.sentence: NHS inform says being unable to pass any urine is a medical emergency and to phone 999 for an ambulance.
entries.note: As in body section ledger entries.

entries.sentence: The prostate is a small gland below the bladder in men.
entries.note: Prostatitis summary: a small gland below the bladder in men.

entries.sentence: For an enlarged prostate, the NHS describes urinary problems as the main sign.
entries.note: NHS summaries: urinary problems the main sign of enlarged prostate.

entries.sentence: These include trouble starting to pee, a weak flow, dribbling after finishing and needing to go more often, especially at night.
entries.note: Weak flow, difficulty starting, dribbling after, more often at night (Prostate Cancer UK/NHS summaries).

entries.sentence: Some men with an enlarged prostate have no symptoms at all.
entries.note: Some men do not get any symptoms.

entries.sentence: The NHS says the symptoms usually build slowly and may get worse as a man gets older.
entries.note: Quote: symptoms usually develop slowly and may gradually get worse with age.

entries.sentence: Prostatitis, which is inflammation of the prostate, can cause pain or stinging when passing urine, straining to pass urine and needing to go more often.
entries.note: NHS 111 Wales/NHS: pain or stinging, difficulty or straining, more often.

entries.sentence: It can also cause pain in the penis, scrotum, testicles or bottom.
entries.note: Same list: pain in penis, scrotum, testicles or bottom.

entries.sentence: Sudden bacterial cases can bring a high temperature, sweating, chills and pain between the testicles and the back passage.
entries.note: Search summary (blended) described acute bacterial cases with these; attributed to Prostate Cancer UK page, not confirmed page-level.

entries.sentence: The NHS says early prostate cancer often causes no symptoms.
entries.note: Early prostate cancer often causes no symptoms.

entries.sentence: Later signs can include peeing problems, lower back pain, tiredness and weight loss.
entries.note: Later signs listed.

entries.sentence: The NHS says it is not clear what causes benign prostate enlargement, but it is thought to be linked to hormone changes as men get older.
entries.note: Quote: not clear what causes it; thought linked to hormone changes with ageing.

entries.sentence: Prostate Cancer UK lists age, hormonal changes, a family history of enlarged prostates and other health conditions as possible factors.
entries.note: Quote of causes list.

entries.sentence: The NHS says prostatitis is usually caused by an infection, such as a urinary tract infection.
entries.note: Prostatitis usually caused by infection such as UTI.

entries.sentence: It is not always known what causes long-term prostatitis.
entries.note: Not always known for chronic prostatitis.

entries.sentence: The NHS adds that needing to pee often at night or having a weak flow is common in older men and does not necessarily mean cancer.
entries.note: Search summary: such symptoms common in older men and do not necessarily mean cancer.

entries.sentence: An enlarged prostate is not prostate cancer, and Prostate Cancer UK says it does not raise the risk of prostate cancer.
entries.note: Quote: not prostate cancer and does not increase risk.

entries.sentence: A man can have both at the same time.
entries.note: Men can have both at the same time.

entries.sentence: The NHS says most men with prostate symptoms do not have prostate cancer, though symptoms can sometimes be caused by more serious conditions, including cancer.
entries.note: NHS notes most men with prostate symptoms do not have cancer; symptoms can sometimes be caused by more serious conditions such as prostate cancer.

entries.sentence: Blood in the urine may be a symptom of an enlarged prostate, but the NHS says this is rare and it is usually caused by something else.
entries.note: Quote: may be a symptom but rare and usually caused by something else.

entries.sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP for difficulty peeing, needing to pee more often, blood in the pee, pain when peeing or not being able to pee at all.
entries.note: NHS enlarged prostate page list of reasons to get a GP appointment.

entries.sentence: It also advises seeing a GP if symptoms change, get worse or do not feel normal.
entries.note: Search summary: see a GP if symptoms change, get worse, or do not feel normal.

entries.sentence: A urologist writing for NHS England said men with intrusive urinary symptoms should see their GP for assessment and, if needed, referral.
entries.note: Urologist article: if intrusive, see GP for assessment and if necessary referral.

entries.sentence: For blood in the pee, pain when peeing or being unable to pee, the NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111.
entries.note: NHS enlarged prostate page: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for these.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a GP asks about symptoms and how they affect daily life.
entries.note: GP asks about symptoms and daily-life impact.

entries.sentence: The GP may examine the tummy and genital area, and may feel the prostate through the wall of the back passage, which is called a rectal examination.
entries.note: Examination of abdomen and genitals; rectal examination.

entries.sentence: A urine sample may be tested for infection.
entries.note: GP may test urine sample for infection.

entries.sentence: A blood test may check that the kidneys are working properly, and a PSA blood test may also be offered.
entries.note: Blood test for kidneys; PSA test may be offered.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a PSA result cannot give a definite diagnosis of prostate cancer.
entries.note: PSA test cannot provide a definitive diagnosis of prostate cancer.

entries.sentence: Men are usually asked to keep a diary of what they drink and how often and how much they pee.
entries.note: Symptom diary of drinking and peeing.

entries.sentence: A specialist may see men whose prostate feels abnormal or whose PSA result is raised.
entries.note: Referral if PSA raised or prostate feels abnormal.

entries.sentence: Hospital tests can include a urine flow test, an ultrasound scan of the bladder and a camera test of the bladder called cystoscopy.
entries.note: Urine flow test, bladder ultrasound, cystoscopy.

entries.sentence: If prostate cancer is suspected, the NHS says the next steps can include an MRI scan and sometimes a biopsy.
entries.note: Search summary: MRI scan then a biopsy may follow.

entries.sentence: The NHS says treatment depends on how much the symptoms affect daily life.
entries.note: Treatment depends on how much symptoms affect daily life.

entries.sentence: Mild symptoms may need only monitoring, which is often called watchful waiting.
entries.note: Mild cases often need monitoring, called watchful waiting.

entries.sentence: Lifestyle changes can include drinking less alcohol, caffeine and fizzy drinks, drinking less in the evening, exercising and keeping to a healthy weight.
entries.note: Lifestyle list from search summary.

entries.sentence: Medicines include alpha-blockers such as tamsulosin, which relax the muscles of the bladder and prostate.
entries.note: Alpha-blockers such as tamsulosin relax bladder and prostate muscles.

entries.sentence: Another group, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors such as finasteride, shrink the gland over time.
entries.note: Finasteride and dutasteride shrink the gland over time.

entries.sentence: Surgery is generally kept for symptoms that do not respond to medicines, and UK options include transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), HoLEP, water vapour therapy and GreenLight laser surgery.
entries.note: Surgery generally for symptoms not responding to medicine; UK types listed.

entries.sentence: For sudden bacterial prostatitis, the NHS says treatment is with antibiotics.
entries.note: Acute bacterial prostatitis treated with antibiotics.

entries.sentence: For long-term prostatitis, a GP may refer a man to a urologist, and treatment can include medicines, physiotherapy or talking therapies.
entries.note: Chronic cases: referral to urologist; medicines, physiotherapy or talking therapies.

entries.sentence: Being unable to pass any urine at all is called acute urinary retention.
entries.note: AUR is sudden inability to pass any urine.

entries.sentence: NHS inform treats it as a medical emergency, because urine backing up can damage the kidneys, and says to phone 999 for an ambulance.
entries.note: Quote: medical emergency; kidneys; phone 999 and ask for an ambulance.

entries.sentence: Other signs it lists include severe lower tummy pain and a swollen bladder that can be felt.
entries.note: Lists severe lower abdominal pain and bladder swelling you can feel.

entries.sentence: A hospital leaflet says a man in this situation needs to attend an emergency department to have a catheter put in.
entries.note: Sussex leaflet: attend emergency department to have a catheter inserted.

entries.sentence: The NHS enlarged prostate page gives the route as an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.
entries.note: NHS page: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for cannot pee at all.

entries.sentence: The NHS says prostatitis can be serious and can need urgent medical help.
entries.note: Prostatitis can be serious and needs urgent medical help.

entries.sentence: A fever alongside urinary symptoms can point to a serious infection or sepsis.
entries.note: NHS notes such symptoms with fever can point to serious infection or sepsis.
